headline: Police and residents discussed a proposed ban on Flock license plate cameras; the ordinance remains under review.
summary: Police explained how they use license plate readers in stolen vehicle, violent crime, and missing person cases, and Flock Safety answered questions on data storage and sharing. Residents raised privacy concerns and differing views on the technology. A follow-up meeting was discussed for November 17, 2026.

Public Portion 
 1. Review and Discussion of the Draft Ordinance Prohibiting Automated License Plate 
Reader Systems (Flock Cameras). 
On November 4, 2026, the Public Safety Committee, chaired by Councilor Gerry Martin, met to 
review and discuss the proposed ordinance prohibiting Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) 
systems, commonly known as Flock cameras. Councilor Zaida Govan, sponsor of the proposed 
ordinance, outlined concerns regarding individual privacy, surveillance, data security, and 
potential misuse of information collected through the technology. Springfield Police 
Superintendent Lawrence Akers, accompanied by Police Department representatives, explained 
the department's current use of ALPR technology in investigations involving stolen vehicles, 
violent crimes, missing persons, and other public safety matters. Police officials described 
existing departmental policies, access restrictions, auditing procedures, and oversight measures 
intended to prevent unauthorized use. 
 
A representative from Flock Safety addressed questions regarding data ownership, storage, 
retention, cybersecurity, and information-sharing practices. Councilors and residents raised 
concerns about potential access by outside agencies, unauthorized surveillance, the distribution 
of cameras throughout Springfield neighborhoods, and the transparency of the City's contracting 
and implementation process. Police officials maintained that Springfield's system is subject to 
restrictive policies and that searches require an authorized investigative purpose and 
corresponding case or service number. Discussion also addressed the effectiveness of ALPR 
technology in criminal investigations, the distinction between license plate readers and other 
surveillance cameras, and the importance of balancing public safety with constitutional privacy 
protections. Residents expressed differing perspectives regarding the benefits and risks of 
continued use. 
 
Councilor Martin emphasized the importance of continued public discussion and indicated that 
the committee would further examine the proposed ordinance and its potential implementation. 
A tentative follow-up Public Safety Committee meeting was discussed for Tuesday, November 
17, 2026, at 4:30 p.m., to focus more specifically on the ordinance and allow additional public 
input. Councilor Martin also expressed interest in visiting the Police Department to better 
understand the technology and its operation. No formal vote or recommendation to the full City 
Council was recorded, and the proposed ordinance remained under committee review. The 
meeting adjourned at 5:43 p.m.
